transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-05-11
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 44 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Karen Patel (Novus Head of ML), Omar Reyes (Platform Eng), Lydia Cho (Security)

Auto-summary: Intro demo focused on multi-tenant quotas, org/project key patterns, and fairness during bursts. Discussed hosted vs dedicated, VPC/KMS concerns, and next steps for a small scale POC.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on this account. we also have Diego from the engineering team. how's Novus doing today?
[00:07] Karen: Hi Maya, good, thanks. we've been trying to stabilize our generative recommendations traffic, spikes at noon are killing our response times and cost is creeping up.
[00:18] Diego: cool—sounds familiar. quick agenda: walk through org/project key patterns, show the Console quota UI, the API behaviors for fairburst, and a quick Optimize suggestion for batching and kv cache. we'll pause for questions.
[00:30] Omar: quick ask up front: we are on a hybrid infra, currently using CloudModelX endpoints and some in-house GPU pools. our main concerns are tenant isolation, predictable SLOs, and encryption at rest - KMS integration.
[00:44] Lydia: and from security we need audit logs, SSO (SAML), and evidence for SOC2 controls.
[00:52] Maya: great, we'll cover those. at high level, Redwood offers (1) hosted with org/project key zoning and quotas, (2) dedicated reserved pools, and (3) private VPC deployments for stricter controls. many customers start hosted with strict quotas then move to dedicated when they need latency guarantees.
[01:12] Karen: can you explain the org vs project key pattern again? we have teams that want isolated budgets but others want shared throughput.
[01:21] Diego: sure. org-key is top-level, gives global quotas and billing. project-keys are scoped under an org for teams or features. you can assign concurrency quotas per key, burst windows, and set fairshare so noisy projects don't starve others. with token-level routing you can pin critical routes to higher priority lanes.
[01:39] Omar: how deterministic is fairshare during a sharp spike? like if marketing runs a campaign and bursts 10x for a minute.
[01:46] Diego: fairshare uses a leaky-bucket per key combined with project slices. during a sustained spike, requests above quota are queued briefly up to a soft limit then either throttled or routed to a lower-cost model variant. it's tunable. we've seen median latency remain stable for 60s spikes in our internal tests, but depends on model size and KV cache hit rate.
[02:08] Karen: you mentioned routing to model variants—do you mean you fallback to smaller quantized models automatically?
[02:14] Maya: yes, policy-driven fallback. you can define a policy: e.g., prefer rdx-large, fallback to rdx-small-q4 when under capacity pressure. Optimize can recommend which variants based on cost/quality tradeoffs.
[02:27] Lydia: on encryption—KMS/HSM—how do we ensure customer-managed keys for private deploy?
[02:33] Diego: for private deployments, we integrate with your KMS. keys never leave your environment, and logs can be shipped to your SIEM. hosted also supports envelope encryption + optional customer-managed keys for certain plans. i'll share the security runbook link after.
[02:47] Omar: latency numbers? we need p95 under 220ms for short chat usecases. currently avg of CloudModelX is around 400ms under load.
[02:55] Diego: depends on model and batching. with RDX-medium on dedicated capacity and optimized kernels, p95 for 1-shot generate with 64 tokens was 180ms in our benchmark with warm KV cache. cold-start and long contexts will be higher. we'll run a targeted POC with your payloads to validate.
[03:15] Karen: how does the Console show quotas? can product managers adjust limits without asking infra?
[03:22] Maya: Console has an Org Quotas page—admin roles can edit project slices, set rate limits, and preview the cost impact. we also have role-based access control so only PMs with assigned roles can change runtime quotas.
[03:36] Karen: nice. during the demo please show how to set a burst policy and tie it to project keys.
[03:41] Diego: sure—i'll share my screen. (screen share) okay, Console > Governance > Quota policies. here you can create a policy, set tokens/sec, concurrent requests, and a burst allowance for X seconds. you can also attach a fallback model list.
[04:02] (short pause, typing noises)
[04:08] Diego: i'm creating a policy named "marketing-burst-control". set baseline to 200 req/min, burst +500 for 120s, fairshare group: projects tagged marketing. you can see a preview of the simulated impact on latency and cost—this is from our simulator, not live traffic. sometimes the simulator underestimates cold cache impact.
[04:34] Omar: how are project tags synced? we have Terraform-managed infra.
[04:39] Maya: we have an API to create projects and tags. many customers integrate via IaC (Terraform) — we can provide a module. we'll include a sample in the follow-up.
[04:52] Karen: question about billing—if we route to fallback models during spikes, how does cost attribution work?
[04:58] Diego: billing is per-model per-token; Console shows per-route/mode breakdown. you can also set a budget alert per project. if fallback is used, cost shows up under the project key that originated the request.
[05:12] Lydia: audit logs—do you provide token-level tracing or just aggregated metrics?
[05:17] Diego: we provide request-level metadata (no raw prompt unless you opt-in) for traces, with full audit events for config changes. logs can be exported to your S3/GCS or SIEM. data retention policies configurable.
[05:31] Karen: what about throttling behavior—do you return 429 instantly or queue?
[05:35] Diego: you can choose: hard reject (429) or soft-queue with a small wait (we expose retry-after headers). soft-queue helps preserve user experience for brief spikes but increases tail latency slightly.
[05:49] Omar: security reviewed by third-party? we need SOC2 Type II evidence and pen test reports.
[05:55] Maya: yes—we have SOC2 Type II and recent pen test summary. i'll attach the security pack.
[06:02] Karen: what's the expected time to get a POC running? we have a marketing campaign in three weeks.
[06:07] Maya: we can set up a staging org and baseline tests within 5 business days, then run a week-long spike sim. for SLA-level deterministic latency you might need Dedicated capacity which has a procurement lead time (depends on contract), but for initial validation, hosted + quotas should be fast.
[06:28] Lydia: any known limitations with our hybrid cloud setup?
[06:31] Diego: if you want private network connectivity, VPC peering and private endpoints are supported in Private mode. there are some networking lags when connecting to on-prem HSMs—we've seen extra RTTs. we'll document the typical ranges.
[06:45] Karen: can Optimize auto-suggest quantization vs batching tradeoffs per endpoint?
[06:50] Diego: yes—Optimize analyzes your token distribution and suggests quantization profiles and batching windows. it flags potential quality regressions on a small eval set. it's a recommendation engine, you still control rollouts.
[07:03] Maya: quick demo of API behavior: POST /v1/generate with project_key header. you can see rate-limit headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset. also X-Fairshare-Rank when fairshare applied.
[07:18] Omar: will our engineers need to rewrite SDK calls?
[07:22] Diego: minimal change—just include project_key header and handle 429/retry-after. SDKs already have helpers.
[07:29] (short cross talk)
[07:34] Karen: any objections or tradeoffs we should know? e.g., price vs p95?
[07:38] Maya: yes—the main tradeoff is latency vs cost. smaller quantized models reduce tokens cost and GPU usage but can increase inference time slightly on some hardware and may impact answer quality. batching improves throughput and cost but increases per-request latency, which may not be acceptable for user-facing chat.
[07:58] Omar: can we do per-customer quotas within a single project? some features are multi-tenant themselves.
[08:04] Diego: yes—you can have sub-keys or hashed client-ids with per-subquota enforcement. that's a common pattern for marketplace-style apps.
[08:14] Karen: what's the rollback story if a fallback impacts quality badly in a live run?
[08:19] Diego: we recommend canarying fallback policies (5-10% traffic), paired with eval monitors. Console can auto-abort rollouts if quality regressions exceed thresholds on saved eval prompts.
[08:33] Maya: sounds like we've covered core items. quick recap and next steps?
[08:38] Karen: recap sounds good. we'll share traffic samples and our key hierarchy by Friday.
[08:43] Maya: i'll send pricing and security docs; Diego will share the recording and sample Terraform module.
[08:49] Omar: ok let's target the POC kickoff next Tuesday.
[08:52] Lydia: one last note: please include the data-retention options in the security pack.
[08:57] Maya: will do. thanks everyone.

(End of transcript)

References and links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/docs/security, https://redwood.ai/console/quota-policies, sample Terraform module: https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules (note: link placeholder).
